source_text: Ὁ δ᾽ ἡμέτερος οὗτος, ἔστω χαριστήριος ἀνθρώπων μὲν πάντων μάλιστα, τῷ ἀνδρὶ τῷ ἱερῷ τῷδε. εἰ δέ τι καὶ περαιτέρω μεγαληγορεῖν ἐθέλοιμι, καὶ τῶν οὐ φαινομένων μὲν, θειοτέρων δὲ, καὶ κηδομένων ἀνθρώπων, τούτῳ ὅς με ἐκ παίδων κρίσει τινὶ μεγάλῃ οἰκονομεῖν τε καὶ τιθηνεῖσθαι καὶ ἐπιτροπεύειν ἐκληρώσατο, ὁ ἱερὸς ἄγγελος Θεοῦ· ὁ τρέφων με ἐκ νεότητός μου, φησὶν ἐκεῖνος ὁ Θεῷ φίλος ἀνὴρ τὸν αὐτοῦ λέγων δηλαδή. ἀλλ᾽ ὁ μὲν μέγας ὢν, ἀναλόγως μέγαν τινὰ ἤτοι ἄλλον ὅστις ἂν ἐκεῖνος ᾖ, ἢ καὶ αὐτὸν ἴσως τὸν τῆς μεγάλης βουλῆς ἄγγελον, τὸν κοινὸν πάντων σωτῆρα, ὑπὸ τελειότητος μόνον ἤδη φύλακα αὐτῷ εἶναι κληρωσάμενος, οὐκ οἶδα τοῦτο σαφῶς. πλὴν ὁ μὲν, τὸν ἑαυτοῦ μέγαν τινὰ, ὅς τις ποτ᾽ ἂν ᾖ, καὶ γινώσκων καὶ εὐφημῶν. ἡμεῖς δὲ πρὸς τῷ κοινῷ πάντων ἀνθρώπων κυβερνήτῃ, καὶ τοῦτον ὅς τίς ποτ᾽ ἐστὶν ἰδίᾳ παιδαγωγὸς ἡμῶν ὄντα ἐκ νηπίων. ὅς τά τε ἄλλα πάντῃ πάντα ἀγαθὸς ὢν τροφεὺς καὶ κηδεμὼν ἐμὸς, (οὐχὶ ἐμοὶ ἢ τινὶ τῶν ἐμοὶ προσηκόντων φίλων· τυφλοὶ γὰρ ἡμεῖς καὶ μηδὲν τῶν ἔμπροσθεν ὁρῶντες, ὥστε τι καὶ κρίνειν δύνασθαι τῶν δεόντων· ἀλλ᾽ ἢ αὐτῷ προορωμένῳ πάντα τὰ πρὸς ὠφέλειαν τῆς ψυχῆς ἡμῶν, συμφέρον εἶναι καταφαίνεται.) πάλαι τε καὶ νῦν ἔτι ἐκτρέφει τε καὶ χειραγωγεῖ. καὶ δὴ πρὸς πᾶσι τοῖς ἄλλοις, καὶ συνάψαι με τῷ ἀνδρὶ τούτῳ. τοῦτο δὴ τὸ κεφαλαιωδέστατον πάντων, ἐμηχανήσατο, οὔτε γένει καὶ αἵματί με ἀνθρωπίνῳ τινὶ προσήκοντα, οὔτε ἄλλως προσήκοντα, ἢ ὄντα τινὰ τῶν πλησιοχώρων, οὔτε καὶ ὁμοεθνῆ ὅλως. ταῦτα δὴ ἃ προφάσεις φιλίας καὶ ἑνώσεως τοῖς πολλοῖς τῶν ἀνθρώπων γίνεται· ἀλλὰ συνελόντα εἰπεῖν, ἀγνῶτας, ἀλλοτρίους, ἀπεξενωμένους, ἀλλήλων ἀφεστηκότας πάμπολυ, ὅσον μέσα ἔθνη καὶ ὄρη, καὶ ποταμοὶ διείργειν ἡμᾶς, ὑπὸ τῆς θείας ὄντως καὶ σοφῆς προμηθείας εἰς ταὐτὸν ἀγαγὼν, τὴν σωτήριον ἐμοὶ συνόδον ταύτην ἐμηχανήσατο. ἄνωθεν τοῦτο προμηθούμενος οἶμαι ἐκ πρώτης γενέσεως καὶ ἀνατροφῆς. πῶς δὲ μακρὸν ἂν εἴη διεξιέναι, οὐχὶ ἀκριβολογουμένῳ μόνον καὶ μηδὲν παραλιπεῖν πειρωμένῳ· ἀλλ᾽ εἰ καὶ τὰ πολλὰ παρεὶς, ἀθρόως, ὀλίγον τῶν κεφαλαιωδεστέρων μνημονεύειν ἐθελήσαιμι.
thought_title: The guardian angel who has led him from childhood
orientation: Gregory gives thanks to Origen and to the guardian angel who has led him since childhood.
pass_a_gloss: But this [speech] of ours, let it be thank-offering, of all ἄνθρωποι most of all, to this sacred man. And if I would wish to boast further, also [to one] of those not visible but more divine and caring for men, to this one who from childhood by some great judgment was allotted to manage, to nurse and to be guardian of me, the holy angel of God; 'ὁ τρέφων με ἐκ νεότητός μου' (he who feeds me from my youth), says that man dear to God, meaning clearly his own. But he being μέγας, proportionately some great one — either another, whoever he may be, or perhaps the very Angel of Great Counsel, the common Savior of all, by reason of perfection now as sole guardian to him having been allotted — I do not know this clearly. But he, his own great one, whoever he may be, both knowing and praising; we, besides the common governor of all men, also this one, whoever he is, personal tutor of ours from infancy; who being in all else in every way good nurse and guardian of mine — — of old and still now nurtures and leads by the hand. And besides all else, to join me to this man, this the most important of all, he contrived: me neither by γένος and human blood related, nor otherwise related, nor one of the neighbors, nor of the same nation at all; these being occasions of friendship and union to most men; but to say briefly, unknown, strangers, estranged, standing apart from each other very far, as far as intervening nations, mountains and rivers to separate us, by the truly divine and wise providence bringing together, ἐμηχανήσατο this saving meeting for me; from above, from the start foreseeing this, I think, from first birth and upbringing. How, it would be long to go through, not only for one speaking precisely and trying to omit nothing, but even if, passing over the many, summarily, I should wish to recall a few of the more important.

pass_b_english: But let this speech of ours be a thank-offering, among all people, most of all to this holy man. And if I should wish to speak still more boldly, let it also be thanks to one of those beings who are not seen but are more divine, and who care for human beings: to him who, by some great judgment, was given charge of me from childhood, to manage, nurse and guard me, the holy angel of God, “who has fed me from my youth” (Genesis 48:15–16), as that man who was dear to God says, meaning, of course, his own.

He, being great, had a correspondingly great guardian: whether some other, whoever that may be, or perhaps the Angel of Great Counsel himself (Isaiah 9:6), the common Savior of all, whom, by reason of his perfection, he had by then received as his only guardian. This I do not know clearly. In any case, he knew and praised his own great one, whoever he may be. We, besides the common Governor of all people, acknowledge and praise also this one, whoever he is, who has been our own tutor from infancy. In everything else he has been in every way my good nurse and guardian, not as seems beneficial to me or to any of the friends close to me, for we are blind and see nothing of what lies ahead, so as to be able to judge anything of what is needed, but as seems beneficial to him, who foresees everything that helps our soul. Long ago and still now he nurtures me and leads me by the hand.

And besides all this, he contrived to join me to this man, the most important thing of all. I was not related to him by family or human blood, nor connected in any other way, nor one of his neighbors, nor even of the same nation at all, the very things that give most people their grounds for friendship and union. To put it shortly, we were unknown to each other, strangers, foreign to each other, standing very far apart, as far as the nations, mountains and rivers in between could separate us. Yet he brought us together by a providence truly divine and wise, and contrived this saving meeting for me, foreseeing it from above, I think, from my first birth and upbringing. How he did so would take long to recount, not only for one who speaks with precision and tries to leave nothing out, but even if I were to pass over most of it and chose to recall, in brief, a few of the most important points.
notes: 'Who has fed me from my youth' quotes Jacob's blessing (Genesis 48:15 LXX, ὁ τρέφων με ἐκ νεότητος), where the next verse names 'the angel who redeems me from all evils' (48:16); both verses are cited because Gregory reads the feeder as Jacob's angel. 'The Angel of Great Counsel' (τῆς μεγάλης βουλῆς ἄγγελος) is the Septuagint wording of Isaiah 9:6 (verse 9:5 in Hebrew and Rahlfs numbering; English Bibles read 'Wonderful Counsellor'); cited by English numbering. Doubtful readings in the print: 'φύλακα αὐτῷ' (abbreviated pronoun; could be αὐτοῦ, same sense); 'γινώσκων καὶ εὐφημῶν' (endings abbreviated; taken as participles with Jacob as subject). 'Whom ... he had by then received as his only guardian' renders μόνον ἤδη φύλακα ... κληρωσάμενος: μόνον is accusative and goes with the guardian, not with Jacob (Latin column 'solum iam perfectionis gratia custodem adeptus', page image PDF 78 checked). The parenthesis (οὐχὶ ἐμοὶ ... συμφέρον εἶναι καταφαίνεται) is rendered 'not as it seemed best to me ... but as it seemed best to him'. The guardian angel from childhood may recall Matthew 18:10, and 'from my first birth' Galatians 1:15; neither is close enough to cite. The last sentence runs on into the narrative of 5.1.
